name: Sam Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking to me, Sam. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything is confidential. Could you start with a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for CareLoop, a newer home care company in the city that does things a bit differently. Our clients have sensors in their homes, so if someone hasn't opened the fridge by ten, it flags it, and we do video check-ins between visits. My actual day is still five or six visits, washing, meals, tablets, plus fitting and checking the sensor kits. I'm the junior on my team, only a year in, and honestly I'm still worse than the others at the personal care side, I rush it. What I like is the mix of people and gadgets. What wears me out is clients who hate the cameras and take it out on me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you use AI, and what's life like outside work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day, for everything. I talk my notes into the CareLoop app and it writes them up, I ask an AI chat to explain a client's new medicine, I plan my week with it. I live on my own in a rented studio, no partner right now. I left school early but I've always been good with money, I've got more than six months saved and some shares. I also do a side thing on weekends, setting up video doorbells and smart speakers for older people, which pays well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's disappointing, because I was looking forward to it. At CareLoop I'd say we keep doing what we do, sensors and people together. Online I'd probably post something like the hype was ahead of the tech.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine. CareLoop's model works without any big AI leap, and care is short of people anyway. The weekend gadget work would carry on too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my visits and keep the weekend setups going, maybe raise my prices a bit. I'd keep investing a bit each month in an index fund. I'd do the personal care refresher, because I know I rush it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit let down, if anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you rush personal care. Tell me about that.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My team leader Jo watched me do a wash and said I treat it like a checklist. She's right. I can set up a sensor kit in twenty minutes, but I'm still learning not to rush an old man through his shower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do clients say about the cameras?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some love them, their kids can see they're okay. Some feel watched in their own homes, which I get. One lady covers hers with a tea towel every time I leave.

say: I'd post that the **hype** was ahead of the tech.
At CareLoop I'd say we keep combining **sensors and people**.
think: CareLoop's model works without any **big AI leap**, so I'm fine.
My **weekend gadget** work would carry on as well.
do: Keep my visits and raise **weekend setup** prices a bit.
Keep putting money into an **index fund** monthly.
Take the **personal care** refresher because I rush.

fieldNote: He is the rare carer who is **disappointed** by the plateau.
He openly admits he **rushes** personal care, his weak spot.
A weekend **side business** already gives him a second income.

steps.text: Keep doing CareLoop visits and sensor checks
Raise prices for weekend smart doorbell and speaker setups
Put a set amount into the index fund each month
Take the personal care refresher to stop rushing washes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is great for companies like CareLoop and for carers who learn the tools. I'd be honest that some office jobs will go. I'd probably write a long post about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's good for me. I already use the tools every day, and the hands-on work stays because robots are slow. The risk is the company needs fewer of us if AI plans perfect routes and cuts travel time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask CareLoop to put me on the team that tests new tools, and I'd ask for a pay rise for it. I'd grow the weekend business, maybe set up AI reminder systems for older people. I'd keep investing every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited. I like change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the company might need fewer of you. Would that be you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, because I'm the one who likes the tech. If my company needs fewer carers, the ones they keep will be the ones who can work with the software. I'd still need to get better at the actual care, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who might struggle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My colleague Hannah, she's brilliant with clients but hates her phone. I'd try to help her. She's taught me loads about washing people properly.

I'd admit in a **long post** that some office jobs will go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's huge and we need to move fast, both companies and government. I'd say carers should be part of designing how robots go into homes. I'd be all over it online, explaining what it means.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, two years for the thinking AI and 2031 for robots means my visit job goes in about five years. But CareLoop is already talking about piloting robots, and they've asked me to help. I think I'd move into setting up and checking robots, which is close to what I do with sensors. The bit that worries me is whether AGI does that job too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd put my hand up for CareLoop's robot pilot. I'd do an online course in robotics maintenance on evenings. I'd keep building the weekend business, and I'd keep more cash in the bank and less in shares, in case things get bumpy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly excited, a bit uneasy. Like the top of a roller coaster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said AGI might do the robot setup job too. Does that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. A robot that can wash someone can probably fix itself, so the job I'm aiming for might only last a few years. I'd just keep jumping to the next thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grandma, if she were still alive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's why I went into care. I'd tell her I'd make sure the robots were kind. She'd tell me to stop being silly and come for Sunday lunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a good runway if we use it. At work I'd push CareLoop to get ahead of the big firms. Online I'd share what I learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truly, this one suits me best. I can get properly good at care for a few years, learn robotics properly, and be ready for 2034. The thinking AI in 2031 would mostly help me, it already writes my notes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do a proper part-time qualification in robotics or assistive tech over two or three years. I'd keep doing visits and get better at them. I'd keep investing and grow the weekend business into something with a name and a van maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and pretty hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A business with a name and a van. Tell me more.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something like setting up and maintaining home tech for older people, maybe robots later. Give me five years and I'd rather own a small van fixing care robots than wait for one to replace me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong with that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Big companies doing it cheaper, obviously. But older people like someone local who turns up. My savings mean I could survive a slow first year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is loads of time, there's no excuse not to prepare. I'd tell other carers to start learning the tech now. I'd be relaxed about it in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be fine. By 2039 I'd be thirty-seven, with the business going and a qualification. The only risk is me getting lazy with ten years to play with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my CareLoop job for several years and get good at care. I'd do the qualification slowly. I'd keep investing and build the weekend business steadily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Almost too calm, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might get lazy. Is that a real risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. With a deadline I move. Ten years is long enough for me to talk about a plan for nine of them and then panic in the last one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you stop that happening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Set myself dates, like qualified by thirty, business registered by twenty-nine. I'd use the AI to keep me to it, it nags me about everything else already.

fieldNote: His main risk here is his own **procrastination**, which he names himself.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the job I'm aiming for might not last long. What would help is affordable courses in robot maintenance, and companies letting carers like me help design how robots are used.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the cameras. People forget care is about privacy. An old woman covering the camera with a tea towel every time I leave tells you more about care tech than any sales pitch.

headlineQuote: An old woman covering the camera with a tea towel every time I leave tells you more about care tech than any sales pitch.
portrait: Sam is a **27-year-old** junior carer at CareLoop, a sensor-based home care company.
He uses **AI daily** and runs a weekend business setting up home tech for older people.
He is calm in most pictures, and **uneasy** in AGI by 2028 because his next role may not last.
He admits he **rushes** personal care and is still learning from colleagues.
His long-term plan is a **local business** maintaining care tech and robots.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because the robot setup role he is aiming for might not last long.
